items.title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
items.excerpt: OneLake table APIs already let Iceberg-compatible engines discover and read tables in Microsoft Fabric. Today we're taking the next step with two additions: Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) writes through the OneLake table endpoint, now available, and a new additional table metadata API, in preview, for adding descriptions and tags to tables and columns. Together, they make OneLake a place where any engine can not only read data, but also publish it, with the business context people and AI agents need to use it well. Write native Iceberg tables from the engines you already use Until now, the OneLake Iceberg endpoint supported read-only metadata operations. Now, IRC-compatible clients can create native Iceberg tables, commit new snapshots, and request short-lived storage credentials through the same endpoint they already use for reads. That means engines such as PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB can land results directly in OneLake using standard Iceberg tooling, with no custom connectors or copy jobs. It has grown tremendously within the community because it is solving a key problem: lowering the integration tax across data and analytics systems. To understand the integration tax, consider a mid-sized or large organization that wants to perform analytics and data processing. It may use several source systems, an analytics platform such as a warehouse or lakehouse, and yet another platform or vendor for orchestration. Fabric brings together a broad set of analytics capabilities within one platform, which can reduce the number of separate integrations an organization needs to design and operate. items.title: Eventhouse support for OneLake security (Generally Available)
items.excerpt: Security should be consistent wherever you query your data. With OneLake security, you can define access controls once, close to the data, and apply them across supported Microsoft Fabric engines without recreating your security rules for each experience. Today, we’re announcing the general availability of OneLake security support for Eventhouse external tables. When these external tables query data secured by OneLake security, they automatically enforce object-level, column-level, and row-level access controls. This extends the same centrally managed security model to KQL queries, helping you maintain consistent, end-to-end security and governance across analytics experiences. Lakehouse data with Eventhouse power The Eventhouse endpoint for Lakehouses provides a high-performance query layer over data stored in the Lakehouse, bringing the speed and scale of the Eventhouse engine to your existing data without requiring another copy. Because access remains governed by OneLake security, users get Eventhouse performance while your organization maintains a shared, centrally managed security model across Fabric. These references are preserved through Git integration and deployment pipelines, helping teams reuse an eventstream definition across workspaces with environment-specific configuration. items.title: Bringing Rust-native Spark compatibility to Microsoft OneLake with Sail and LakeSail
items.excerpt: Coauthor: Shehab Amin Microsoft OneLake gives every Microsoft Fabric tenant a single, unified data lake built on open formats. One copy of data, many engines: that is the promise, and it is what makes OneLake such a strong foundation for analytics and AI alike. This post looks at how Sail , the open-source distributed compute framework, and LakeSail Cloud , the managed platform for running Sail in production, connect natively to OneLake, and what that unlocks for teams running Spark and Python workloads on Fabric. Sail is a drop-in replacement for Apache Spark, rebuilt from the ground up in Rust, with Rust-native support for Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg out of the box. That makes it a natural fit for OneLake, where lakehouse tables are stored in exactly these open formats. Point Sail at a Fabric lakehouse and it reads and writes the same tables the rest of Fabric uses, with no data copies, no extra connectors to install, and no changes to existing Spark code. One engine for data and AI Sail implements the Spark Connect protocol, the gRPC interface that decouples Spark clients from the engine that executes their plans. Existing Spark SQL and DataFrame code targeting Spark 3.5 or 4.

Both the programs and the data live in the file system. Now apply that model to data engineering: OneLake is the file system, Fabric engines are the programs, and the AI prompt is your terminal. Applications in restricted networks need real-time analytics without a route to the public internet. They can publish directly to a custom endpoint source through the workspace’s private connection, bringing these workloads into the same private networking model as supported connector-based sources. What is workspace-level private connectivity? Private Link is a network security feature of the Fabric platform that provides a private connection between a virtual network and Fabric. items.title: Access versioned lakeFS data from Microsoft Fabric with Microsoft OneLake shortcuts
items.excerpt: Coauthor: Iddo Avneri (Treeverse) Use a live branch for up-to-date analytics or pin a shortcut to an immutable commit when reproducibility matters. Data teams often need two seemingly conflicting things: immediate access to the latest data and the ability to return to the exact data behind an earlier analysis, report, or experiment. Maintaining both typically means creating snapshots, copying datasets, or building additional pipelines. That adds operational overhead and makes it harder to know which version of the data was used. Microsoft OneLake and lakeFS provide a simpler, complementary pattern for addressing this use case. OneLake shortcuts allow Microsoft Fabric lakehouses to reference data in external storage through a unified namespace. Because lakeFS exposes versioned data through an S3-compatible gateway , Fabric can access lakeFS-managed datasets by using a OneLake S3-compatible shortcut. The result: Fabric users can access either the current data on a lakeFS branch or an immutable version from a specific commit. items.title: Introducing the data engineering agent for Fabric (Project Osmos)
items.excerpt: AI coding assistants are excellent at turning natural-language transformation instructions into code. For data engineers, the harder question is whether that code produces results they can trust. You can describe transformation logic in natural language, and an AI coding assistant will happily generate hundreds of lines of Spark code. Impressive. But a Spark job can execute successfully and still produce completely wrong results. The logic may work for a subset of the data but fail when run against the full dataset. The pipeline's logic and validation checks may not account for future changes to the data or schema. Incremental loads can cause duplicates. Revenue numbers might look perfectly reasonable until someone reconciles them against the source. Anyone who's spent time working with real-world enterprise data knows that automating data engineering with AI comes with a unique set of challenges. Data engineering involves more than code: it requires working with large datasets and retaining context about their schemas, relationships, and business rules over time.
